content: Certain molecules or ions are transported either through the bloodstream or across the cell membrane. Some of the carriers involved in this process are water-soluble proteins, which may or may not interact with biological membranes. For instance, some carriers transport small hydrophobic molecules, while others are integral transmembrane proteins embedded within the cell membrane. Carrier proteins located in the cell membrane facilitate the movement of substances either into or out of the cell. This transport occurs along the concentration gradient through facilitated diffusion or against the gradient via active transport. Each carrier protein is highly specific, designed to recognize and bind to only one particular substance or a group of closely related substances. The molecule or ion to be transported, referred to as the substrate, must first bind to a specific binding site on the carrier protein. This binding occurs with a certain level of affinity. Once the substrate binds to the carrier protein, and while the binding site is oriented outward, the carrier protein captures or encloses the substrate within its molecular structure. This process results in an internal translocation, where the carrier protein reorients itself so that the binding site now faces the opposite side of the membrane. At this new orientation, the substrate is released from the carrier protein at the binding site on the other side of the membrane. The release is determined by the binding affinity at that site. Importantly, all steps in this transport process are reversible. Examples of such transport mechanisms include: The diffusion of sugars, amino acids, and nucleosides. The uptake of glucose into cells.
